summary: For ages 4–6, help children represent the same small quantity (to 20) in multiple ways — concrete objects (counters/cubes/fingers), pictures (dots, tallies, ten-frames), on a number line, and as a numeral — and translate fluently between them, grasping that every face means the SAME amount. Follow concrete → pictorial → abstract (CPA): show, then draw, then locate on the line and match the numeral, keeping the faces side by side. Introduce the number line via a numbered TRACK of discrete squares before a continuous line, and a marked line before a blank one. Have children CREATE representations, not just read them.
misconceptions: Treating each representation as a separate task rather than the same quantity in different clothes.
Number-line errors: starting at 1 not 0, or counting the marks/gaps incorrectly; treating the line as a picture rather than a measured, ordered scale (the early 'number-line-as-picture' seed).
Drawing an inexact picture or miscounting tallies so the pictorial doesn't match the quantity.
Believing the numeral is 'the real number' and objects/pictures are not (or vice versa).

activities.title: Five shown four ways, driven from any face
steps: Set a small number (to 20) and see it at once as counters, a dotty picture (or tally/ten-frame), a point on a number line, and the numeral card.
Add or remove one counter and watch the picture gain or lose a dot, the number-line marker move one step, and the numeral change to match.
Drive the change from a DIFFERENT face: slide the number-line marker, or add a tally, and watch the other three faces re-form to match.
Say aloud 'these all show ___' each time, naming the quantity after a change.
Switch the number line between numbered-track mode (discrete squares) and continuous-line mode, and between a marked line and a blank one.
activities.insight: A quantity has many faces — blocks, dots, a spot on the line, a symbol — and when the amount changes, every face must change to match, because they all show the same amount in different clothing.

activities.title: Build it, draw it, place it (child creates every face)
steps: Given a target number (≤10 for younger children, to 20 later), build it with counters or cubes — fingers work well for numbers up to ten.
Draw a matching picture — exactly that many dots or tally marks, one mark per count word.
Locate and mark the number on a number line, counting the JUMPS from 0 aloud.
Match the numeral card to the set, the picture, and the number-line point, saying they all show the same amount.
activities.insight: The child can PRODUCE a quantity in every mode, not just recognise it, and sees that the picture and number-line point carry the amount just as the objects do.

activities.title: Read the dot: count the jumps from 0
steps: Look at a number line from 0 to 10 with a dot marked on 6; point to the dot and say what number it means and how you know.
Count the JUMPS from 0 aloud, hopping a finger from 0, rather than counting the ticks.
Point to 0 and say what 0 means here — the start, not a step.
Then show the same number with counters and draw a matching picture.
activities.insight: A number-line point is read by counting the steps from 0, which is the start and not itself a step; 0 anchors the measured, ordered scale.

activities.title: Reference wall and match checks
steps: Use a 'number shown four ways' reference the child can tap to name each face (tap the number-line point → 'five'; tap the tally → 'five').
Answer 'which shows 5?' matching tasks across objects, pictures, number line, and numeral.
Use a slider to place a number on the line, or draw a path to mark it.
Discuss probe questions: 'You drew 6 dots and here are 6 counters — how are they the same? how are they different?' and 'If I show you 4 fingers, can you put a dot on the line for that number?'
activities.insight: Being able to name and match each face is a useful naming/reference layer that supports, but does not replace, building and translating for oneself.

checkQuestion: Here is a number line from 0 to 10 with a dot marked on 6. Point to the dot and tell me what number it means and how you know. Now show me that same number using these counters. Last, draw me a picture that shows that number.
checkAnswer: The dot marks 6 — it's 6 steps on from 0. (Places/counts out exactly 6 counters.) (Draws 6 dots or tally marks.) Each way shows the same amount: six.
